props.title: Frances Ha

sections.content: **Frances Ha** (2013) captures the messy reality of millennial life through stunning black-and-white cinematography and Greta Gerwig's magnetic performance. Noah Baumbach's love letter to French New Wave classics like **The 400 Blows** (1959) follows Frances, an aspiring dancer navigating New York's artistic underbelly with infectious optimism despite constant setbacks. The film's DNA carries traces of **Manhattan** (1979) and **Jules and Jim** (1962), but speaks to contemporary anxieties about friendship, career, and identity. Gerwig's Frances pirouettes through life with awkward grace, embodying the spirit of emerging adulthood in the 2010s.

sections.content: The film's exploration of female friendship, particularly between Frances and Sophie (Mickey Sumner), echoes through later works like **Broad City** (2014-2019) and **Girls** (2012-2017). These relationships feel raw and complex, avoiding typical rom-com tropes. The platonic love story at the center proves more compelling than any romantic subplot. Baumbach's direction, influenced by French New Wave techniques, creates an intimate portrait that's both timeless and distinctly modern.

The black-and-white cinematography by Sam Levy transforms New York into a dreamlike playground, recalling **Manhattan** (1979) while establishing its own contemporary visual identity. Frances's journey through various apartments and temporary homes mirrors the rootless existence of many young urban professionals, a theme later explored in films like **The Worst Person in the World** (2021) and **Obvious Child** (2014). sections.content: Frances's struggle with gentrification and artistic ambition in New York connects to a larger cinematic conversation about millennials in urban spaces. Films like **Inside Llewyn Davis** (2013) and **Listen Up Philip** (2014) similarly examine creative pursuits in an increasingly unaffordable city. The authenticity of Frances's financial struggles - including her brief exile to her alma mater as a resident advisor - grounds the film's whimsy in economic reality.
